Art
ärt
v. (second person singular present of be; rendering Hebrew 'attah hu and the verbless clause, Greek ei)
From Saxon eart, the second person singular present of beon, to be. It pairs with thou as are pairs with ye. Distinguish it entirely from the noun art, skill or craft, which is a separate word from Latin ars.

Biblical Definition

Art is the second person singular of the verb to be: thou art, where a plural would require ye are. Because it can only follow thou, it is the verb of every confession and every accusation made to one person. God's first recorded question after the fall uses it: “Where art thou?” (Genesis 3:9) — not an enquiry after information but a summons to account. Peter's confession uses it: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God”, and so does Nathanael's: “Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel”. The risen Christ uses it to indict a whole church in the person of its angel: “I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot” (Revelation 3:15). And the psalmist uses it as the ground of all his petitions: “Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob” (Psalm 44:4). In every case the word fastens an identity on someone. It is the grammar of what a person actually is before God, as opposed to what he says or does, and Scripture is full of it because God deals with persons and not with abstractions.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second person singular of the present tense of the verb to be; used only with thou. In Scripture it is the verb of confession and of indictment — thou art the Christ, thou art the man, thou art neither cold nor hot.

expand to see more

ART, v. [Sax. eart.] The second person singular of the present tense of the substantive verb; as, thou art.

2. It is used only with the pronoun thou; with ye or you the form is are.

3. In the modern style the distinction is lost, you being used with are for both numbers.

4. ART, n. [L. ars, artis.] Skill in performance; a system of rules for effecting a given end. This is a wholly distinct word.

5. In Scripture, Where art thou? Gen. 3; Thou art the Christ, Matt. 16; thou art neither cold nor hot, Rev. 3.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:9 — "And the LORD God called unto Adam, and said unto him, Where art thou?"

John 1:49 — "Nathanael answered and saith unto him, Rabbi, thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel."

Revelation 3:15 — "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot."

Psalm 44:4 — "Thou art my King, O God: command deliverances for Jacob."

Modern Corruption

The confession thou art the Christ is regularly reduced to a statement of personal preference — what Jesus is to me — rather than a statement of what He is in Himself. The verb will not permit it: art asserts being, not sentiment.

expand to see more

A widespread habit of speech in modern religion converts every confession into an autobiography. Jesus is said to be my Saviour, my Lord, what He means to me — and none of that is false, but as a substitute for the objective claim it is a serious loss. Peter did not say that Jesus had come to function as the Christ in his experience. He said Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God, and the Lord replied that flesh and blood had not revealed it. The confession is a statement about the person of Christ that would be true if Peter had never made it, and the believer's part is not to constitute it but to see it.

The same verb makes the Laodicean indictment inescapable. Christ does not tell that church what it feels or what it intends; He tells it what it is — thou art neither cold nor hot, and afterward, wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked. The church's own estimate ran the other way, for it said I am rich, and increased with goods. Between the self-assessment and the verdict of Christ there is no negotiation, and self-knowledge for a Christian begins by accepting His sentence rather than his own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew often has no copula at all, setting two nouns side by side (the LORD my shepherd), or uses the pronoun hu to bind them; Greek uses ei, the second singular of eimi; Saxon eart gives the English form.

expand to see more

Hebrew verbless clause — the ordinary way of saying thou art, by simple apposition without any verb, as in Psalm 44:4.

Hebrew hu (H1931) — he, that one; used as a copula to join subject and predicate where emphasis is wanted.

Greek ei (G1488) — thou art; the second person singular present of eimi, to be.

Greek eimi (G1510) — I am; the same verb that stands behind the divine name in John 8:58.

Saxon eart — the Old English second singular present, preserved by the Authorized Version alongside thou.

Usage

"Of God summoning the hiding sinner to account: Where art thou? (Genesis 3:9)."

"Of confession made to Christ in person: thou art the Son of God; thou art the King of Israel (John 1:49)."

"Of Christ's verdict on a self-satisfied church: thou art neither cold nor hot (Revelation 3:15)."
